bibl.title: Mapping Antiquity in Collaboration: The Digital Periegesis Project

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: What does it take for researchers and digital research infrastructures to collaborate on analysing an ancient narrative of space?
span.quote: Against this backdrop, this paper examines the affordances and challenges in interdisciplinary collaboration between researchers, projects and contemporary digital research infrastructures for the analysis of ancient narratives.

span.label: Argues that pre-modern space is not reducible to coordinates, and that maps should interrogate a narrative rather than illustrate it.
span.quote: The overarching argument presented here is that Digital Periegesis is not simply a collaboration of scholars from different backgrounds and with different skills, which is a standard interdisciplinary practice in Digital Humanities.

span.label: method
span.quote: Additionally, the Digital Periegesis project team is attempting to break new ground in applying linked data methods and tools and, as such, is establishing a new model of collaboration.

span.label: collaborative semantic annotation of ancient spatial narratives
span.quote: Against this backdrop, this paper examines the affordances and challenges in interdisciplinary collaboration between researchers, projects and contemporary digital research infrastructures for the analysis of ancient narratives.

span.label: practice-report
span.quote: This long research paper then discusses scientific collaboration between researchers and research infrastructures more generally, incorporating information about space, time and people into a reflexive process to illuminate change and development as a way of understanding place fully.

span.label: Place is produced by what historical agents did in a space and what they left there, so a toponym with coordinates is not yet a place
span.quote: Rather, space becomes place through interaction with historical agents and the human footprint left on the ground in the form of monuments, religious sites and other infrastructures.

span.label: Reuse runs in both directions: the project takes a TEI text and a shared annotation tool, and returns enriched text and new place records to the infrastructures it borrowed from
span.quote: Examples of such reuse and recycling include yet are not limited to, drawing on other resources, namely Wikidata, to provide URIs; providing the enriched, annotated Pausanias’s text back to the Perseus Digital Library; and returning new place information to the Pleiades structured vocabulary of ancient place data.

span.label: A private instance of the shared tool lets the project reach archaeological databases and annotate at a finer grain than the public version supports
span.quote: At another level, the Digital Periegesis project team hosts a private and customized instance of Recogito in order to make use of actual archaeological databases, such as the German Archaeological Institute’s DAI/ ARACHNE for semantically annotating the more granular aspects of Pausanias's description (temples, statues, etc.).

span.label: Being the heaviest user of a shared tool turns the project's experience into a contribution in its own right, feeding back into that tool's redesign
span.quote: The fact that our use of Recogito is the most extensive, dense and complex application of this platform also goes to underline the value of the experience that we can share with the rest of the DH community, as Recogito itself undergoes a major overhaul.

span.label: The paper states that the systematic structure of GIS - the class of spatial infrastructure its own method is built on - is frequently ill-suited to the uncertainty and ambiguity characteristic of humanities data.
span.note: what this limits: any GIS treatment of humanities material: THE VERY SYSTEMATIC STRUCTURE OF A GIS IS FREQUENTLY ILL-SUITED TO CAPTURING ASPECTS OF UNCERTAINTY AND AMBIGUITY THAT TYPICALLY CHARACTERISE, AND EXPLAIN INTEREST IN, HUMANITIES D[ata]
span.quote: Yet, the very systematic structure of a GIS is frequently ill-suited to capturing aspects of uncertainty and ambiguity that typically characterise, and explain interest in, Humanities data (Gregory–Healey 2007: 641; Harris–Bergeron–Rouse 2011: 228; Dunn 2019).

span.label: The structure that makes a GIS useful is the same structure that cannot hold the uncertainty and ambiguity humanities data is made of
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - the structure that makes the tool useful is the one that excludes the ambiguity
span.quote: Yet, the very systematic structure of a GIS is frequently ill-suited to capturing aspects of uncertainty and ambiguity that typically characterise, and explain interest in, Humanities data (Gregory–Healey 2007: 641; Harris–Bergeron–Rouse 2011: 228; Dunn 2019).

span.label: Contemporary geographic information science and historical ways of describing space are described as potentially incompatible, not merely different
span.note: what this limits: any assumed compatibility of the two traditions: CONTEMPORARY GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SCIENCE AND HISTORICAL MODES OF DESCRIBING SPACE OFTEN APPEAR TO HAVE DISPARATE, EVEN INCOMPATIBLE, VIEWPOINTS OF THE WORLD
span.quote: While contemporary geographic information science and historical modes of describing space often appear to have disparate, even incompatible, viewpoints of the world, there is a growing ecosystem that seeks to remedy the complexity of ancient space.

span.label: The second phase, extending the work from space to time and people, was still ahead at the time of writing
span.note: what this limits: everything beyond space: the extension to time and people belongs to a SECOND PHASE OF THE PROJECT financed from 2022 to 2026, still ahead at the time of writing
span.quote: In the second phase of the project that is financed by the Swedish Research Council from 2022 to 2026 (Vetenskapsrådet 2021-02799) the Digital Periegesis project is set out to investigate descriptions of time and people and to incorporate this to the ongoing Digital Periegesis’s visualisation.

span.label: GIS and spatial analysis carried into the reading of ancient narrative, together with an explicit statement of where the transfer breaks - the formalism cannot hold the uncertainty that makes the material interesting
span.quote: More recently, the spatial analysis of texts via Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is trending as a research method.

span.label: space - as coordinates and toponyms: what a GIS records, and explicitly not what mapping antiquity amounts to
span.quote: Mapping pre-modern space is rarely a matter of documenting toponyms or establishing precise coordinates.

span.label: place - as space that historical agents have acted in and marked: the sense the project is after
span.quote: Rather, space becomes place through interaction with historical agents and the human footprint left on the ground in the form of monuments, religious sites and other infrastructures.

span.label: map - as illustration: a picture accompanying an argument, which the project rejects
span.quote: using maps as visual portals into narratives, as a means to interrogate rather than merely illustrate spatial information

span.label: collaboration - the standard sense: scholars of different backgrounds and skills working together, which the paper says is ordinary DH practice
span.quote: The overarching argument presented here is that Digital Periegesis is not simply a collaboration of scholars from different backgrounds and with different skills, which is a standard interdisciplinary practice in Digital Humanities.

span.label: collaboration - the sense claimed as new: reciprocal exchange with the infrastructures themselves, taking data and tools and giving enriched data back
span.quote: Additionally, the Digital Periegesis project team is attempting to break new ground in applying linked data methods and tools and, as such, is establishing a new model of collaboration.

span.quote: Additionally, the Digital Periegesis project team is attempting to break new ground in applying linked data methods and tools and, as such, is establishing a new model of collaboration.

span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: collaborative semantic annotation of ancient spatial narratives — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: This ecosystem of tools, content and communities about ancient place and space illustrate how collaboration within the field of digital humanities can be an opportunity for scientific discovery.

span.label: builds-on → the Hestia project (Bouzarovski–Barker 2016; Barker–Pelling 2016)
span.quote: Specifically, our project derives directly from the Hestia project’s blended methodological approach to exploring literary geography, which had highlighted ways in which texts organise spatial knowledge, based on relations between places (Bouzarovski–Barker 2016; Barker–Pelling 2016).

span.label: builds-on → spatial humanities (Bodenhamer–Corrigan–Harris 2010)
span.quote: Our project is essentially theoretically and methodologically inspired by the field of spatial humanities (e.g. Bodenhamer–Corrigan–Harris 2010).
